# Capture passkey upgrade HTML before automatic navigation

<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request to our repo. -->

<!-- If this is your first PR in the ASP.NET Core repo, please run through the checklist
below to ensure a smooth review and merge process for your PR. -->

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

Retain passkey upgrade HTML before its automatic continuation can navigate.

## Description

`BlazorWebTemplate_ConditionalPasskeyRegistration` reads the first upgrade response after the page has submitted its continuation form and navigated away. Chromium can discard that response body, producing the `Network.getResponseBody` error documented in [dotnet/aspnetcore#69494](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/69494).

For the failure cases that inspect redisplayed HTML, fetch and retain the first POST response before fulfilling the original browser request. Do not follow redirects during capture; leave GETs and subsequent POSTs on the normal browser path. Preserve the existing status, request, cookie, credential, signaling, and final-navigation assertions. All eight existing theory rows remain; no production code, retry, delay, timeout, or quarantine changes.

Simply moving the body read after the login click would still race the page's automatic navigation. Capturing before delivery provides an explicit ordering guarantee.

**Validation**

- `node <session-files>\passkey-response-repro.cjs` — passed using installed Edge/Chromium 155 and cached Playwright 1.61.0, a loopback server, and the actual template `PasskeySubmit.razor.js`. Baseline: 12/12 runs reproduced the body-read error. Capture: 12/12 passed, covering successful, rejected, pending, and unsupported signaling. Checked initial GET/query handling, continuation POST, cookie deletion, credential-field removal, original response status, redirect, and final page.
- `& <session-files>\validate-passkey-capture.ps1` — passed; the exact C# capture block compiles with nullable checks and warnings as errors against cached Playwright 1.61.0 and existing .NET 10 references.
- `git -c core.longpaths=true diff --check` — passed.
- `. .\activate.ps1; dotnet --version` — blocked: repository SDK `12.0.100-alpha.1.26531.102` is not installed. No tools were installed.
- **Not run:** `BlazorWebTemplate_ConditionalPasskeyRegistration` in the generated ASP.NET application. The repository SDK and matching built product/template artifacts are unavailable. The browser reproduction does not validate persistence or the eight complete C# theory rows, and the API probe does not replace a project build against pinned Playwright 1.62.0. This draft does not claim verified CI remediation.

**Tradeoff:** a small test-only interception is justified by repeated documented failures and a reproduced browser-lifetime mechanism. It retains all failure detection instead of adding retries or weakening assertions. The added response-path complexity is bounded to one response in affected rows; complete generated-application validation remains required before treating the flake as fixed.

Originally prepared in [mmitche/AspNetCore#8](https://github.com/mmitche/AspNetCore/pull/8), now submitted against upstream `main` at the user's request. Implementation and review were assisted by GitHub Copilot.

Fixes #69494

# Fix account-name overflow in web templates

Allow authenticated account names to wrap in generated web templates.

## Description

Enable wrapping for long account identifiers in Blazor, standalone WebAssembly, MVC and Razor Pages templates. Allow account-name containers to grow so wrapped text does not clip or overlap other controls. Reuses Bootstrap utilities where available; no framework or public API changes.

Fixes dotnet/aspnetcore-scenario-tests#166

## Customer Impact

Long authenticated account names cause horizontal scrolling on narrow screens and at enlarged text sizes, including Identity account-management pages. The fix keeps the full name readable and account controls usable in newly generated apps. Existing apps must apply equivalent markup/CSS changes.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

Eleven template markup/CSS files only. Changes enable text wrapping and content-sized containers without changing authentication behavior, framework code, dependencies or public APIs.

## Verification

- [ ] Manual (required)
- [ ] Automated

The original main-branch fix was manually verified in generated Blazor, MVC and Razor Pages apps. In the recorded Blazor reproduction, document width decreased from 416px to 375px in a 375px viewport. Before/after recordings are in #70346.

Existing `BlazorServerIdentityAccessibilityTests` and `RazorPagesIdentityAccessibilityTests` in dotnet/aspnetcore-scenario-tests report the originating overflow findings in `findings.sarif`; no duplicate tests are added here. A fresh external SARIF scan has not been run. This release/11.0 backport has not been built or tested locally; verification checkboxes remain unchecked pending backport validation.

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

Only template contents change; no package metadata or packaging-infrastructure changes.

----

Issues.Title: Stop RedisOutputCacheStore GC loop on dispose
Issues.Body:
# Stop RedisOutputCacheStore GC loop on dispose

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Summary of the changes (Less than 80 chars)

Observe disposal in the Redis output cache store's garbage collection loop.

## Description

`RedisOutputCacheStore.RunGarbageCollectionLoopAsync` awaited `Task.Delay` (~300 s) without a cancellation token. `Dispose` cancels `_disposalCancellation`, but the pending delay ignored it, so for up to ~5.5 minutes the delay's timer kept the loop's state machine, and through it the store, its logger and its options, reachable. When the options capture a host's service provider (e.g. via `ConnectionMultiplexerFactory`), the disposed host stays alive too.

Changes:
- Pass `_disposalCancellation.Token` to `Task.Delay`.
- Treat the resulting `OperationCanceledException` as a normal exit of the loop (otherwise the outer catch would log it as a fatal GC error).
- The loop task is now kept in an internal `GarbageCollectionLoop` property (it was previously discarded) so the test can observe its completion.

Test: `RedisOutputCacheStoreTests.Dispose_EndsGarbageCollectionLoop` constructs a store (no Redis server needed), disposes it, and asserts the loop task completes (within 30 s) with `RanToCompletion` and no error logged. Without the fix the test fails with a `TimeoutException`; with the fix the Redis test project passes (9 passed, 10 existing server-dependent tests skipped).

Fixes #69849

_This PR was prepared with AI assistance; I reviewed and tested the change._

Issues.Title: [API Proposal]: Opt-in explicit server certificate chain presentation in Kestrel
Issues.Body:
## Background and Motivation

<!--
We welcome API proposals! We have a process to evaluate the value and shape of new API. There is an overview of our process [here](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/docs/APIReviewProcess.md). This template will help us gather the information we need to start the review process.
First, please describe the purpose and value of the new API here.
-->

Kestrel passes `HttpsConnectionAdapterOptions.ServerCertificateChain` to `SslStreamCertificateContext.Create` as `additionalCertificates`. These are chain-building candidates, not an authoritative presentation chain. The platform can choose a different path based on the server's local certificate stores.

This matters for cross-signed CAs. Consider two paths:

```text
Old trusted root -> cross-signed new CA -> intermediate -> server certificate
New self-signed root                  -> intermediate -> server certificate
```

The new self-signed root and cross-signed new CA have the same subject and public key but different issuers and certificate fingerprints. A server trusting the new self-signed root can select the shorter path and omit the configured cross-signed certificate. Clients trusting only the old root then cannot validate the presented chain, although the application supplied the certificates needed for those clients.

[dotnet/runtime discussion #114876](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/discussions/114876) describes this behavior on Linux. [Jeremy Barton's reply](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/discussions/114876#discussioncomment-12902872) demonstrates selecting the longer path with a custom `SslCertificateTrust` containing only the old root.

That workaround is useful, but requires application-level TLS customization. It also affects default peer-certificate validation: an mTLS server must separately preserve its intended client-certificate policy with `SslServerAuthenticationOptions.CertificateChainPolicy`. Configuring the outgoing chain should not implicitly change which client certificates the server trusts.

Please add an **opt-in** way to present an explicitly configured chain independently of server-local trust. Preserve existing `ServerCertificateChain` behavior: callers may already rely on platform chain building with unordered, incomplete, or multi-path certificate collections.

## Proposed API

<!--
Please provide the specific public API signature diff that you are proposing. For example:
```diff
namespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http;

public static class HttpResponseWritingExtensions
{
+    public Task WriteAsync(this HttpResponse response, StringBuilder builder);
}
```
You may find the [Framework Design Guidelines](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/coding-guidelines/framework-design-guidelines-digest.md) helpful.
-->

One possible shape is a mode governing the existing collection:

```diff
namespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Https;

+ public enum ServerCertificateChainMode
+ {
+     Build = 0,
+     Explicit = 1,
+ }

public class HttpsConnectionAdapterOptions
{
+    public ServerCertificateChainMode ServerCertificateChainMode { get; set; }
}
```

Names are open for discussion. Proposed semantics:

- `Build` is the default and retains current behavior.
- In `Explicit` mode, `ServerCertificate` supplies the leaf and private key. `ServerCertificateChain` supplies its ordered issuer chain, starting with the leaf's immediate issuer; it does not include the leaf.
- Kestrel preserves the supplied intermediate certificates, including cross-signed CA certificates, without substituting another path from local stores or downloading additional certificates.
- A terminal self-signed root may be supplied but is not transmitted. A cross-signed CA is not removed merely because it shares a subject/public key with a locally trusted self-signed root.
- The supplied chain need not include a self-signed root: clients independently choose their trust anchors.
- Reject malformed or inconsistent sequences rather than silently reverting to platform chain selection. Sequence checking must not require the server to trust the chain or establish that all clients will trust it.
- This setting does not change client-certificate trust, revocation policy, validation callbacks, or acceptable-issuer advertisement.

The intended guarantee is the outgoing chain, not simply a preference for a particular trust anchor. Implementation may require a corresponding runtime API; the existing custom-trust workaround should not be assumed to provide this stronger guarantee on every platform.

## Usage Examples

<!--
Please provide code examples that highlight how the proposed API additions are meant to be consumed.
This will help suggest whether the API has the right shape to be functional, performant and useable.
You can use code blocks like this:
```csharp
// some lines of code here
```
-->

```csharp
listenOptions.UseHttps(https =>
{
    https.ServerCertificate = serverCertificateWithPrivateKey;
    https.ServerCertificateChain = new X509Certificate2Collection
    {
        issuingIntermediate,
        crossSignedNewCa,
    };
    https.ServerCertificateChainMode = ServerCertificateChainMode.Explicit;
});
```

The presented chain is the server certificate, issuing intermediate, and cross-signed new CA, even when the new self-signed root is locally trusted. The client supplies its own old-root trust anchor.

For mTLS, applications retain their existing `ClientCertificateMode`, `ClientCertificateValidation`, and any separately configured `CertificateChainPolicy`. Enabling explicit presentation must not require changing those policies.

Leaving the new property unset continues to use the existing platform-selected chain.

## Alternative Designs

<!--
Were there other options you considered, such as alternative API shapes?
How does this compare to analogous APIs in other ecosystems and libraries?
-->

- **Change `ServerCertificateChain` behavior unconditionally:** simpler API surface, but risks breaking callers relying on chain building and accepting collections that are not explicit ordered chains.
- **A separate explicit-chain property:** could express the distinction without a mode enum, but requires defining precedence/conflicts with `ServerCertificateChain`.
- **Expose a preferred chain-building trust anchor:** implementable using existing runtime APIs for the Linux scenario, but still requests chain building rather than guaranteeing the supplied presentation chain. It must also avoid changing mTLS validation.
- **Expose `ServerCertificateContext` directly:** simplifies supplying a prebuilt context, but existing contexts still use platform chain construction; this alone does not introduce an exact-presentation guarantee.
- **Keep the `OnAuthenticate` workaround:** available today for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, but requires services to coordinate server-chain selection and client-certificate policy. That callback is not supported for HTTP/3.
- **Add an explicit-chain API in `dotnet/runtime`, then consume it in Kestrel:** potentially the cleanest foundation and useful to other `SslStream` consumers. A companion runtime proposal may be necessary to implement the semantics above.

## Risks

<!--
Please mention any risks that to your knowledge the API proposal might entail, such as breaking changes, performance regressions, etc.
-->

- The default must preserve existing behavior; explicit mode intentionally rejects inputs that remain acceptable as chain-building candidates.
- OpenSSL, Schannel, and other TLS backends do not expose identical chain-selection controls. Unsupported configurations must fail clearly, not silently claim explicit mode while selecting another chain.
- Static certificates, configured SNI endpoints, certificate selectors, and HTTP/3 need consistent semantics or clearly documented limitations. A leaf-only selector cannot automatically supply a different explicit chain for each selected certificate.
- Certificate rotation requires refreshing the chain together with the leaf while preserving certificate lifetimes and existing context caching behavior.
- Regression coverage should assert the certificates actually sent, including their identities, with both roots locally trusted and an old-root-only client. It should also verify unchanged mTLS validation and unchanged default-mode behavior.
- This is an API/design proposal, not a commitment to a particular release or servicing backport.

Issues.Title: Introduce Microsoft.AspNetCore.FormData with source-generated form binding
Issues.Body:
Parent epic: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/70364

# Summary

This document proposes adding `Microsoft.AspNetCore.FormData` to ASP.NET Core: a supported form-data reading API, a form-specific metadata and attribute model, and source generation for reading form fields and uploaded files into .NET models. It addresses the lack of supported customization contracts and generated complex-model binding in the implementation currently shared by Blazor static server rendering and Minimal APIs. Applications can describe names, exclusion, construction, culture, empty values, and custom conversions without depending on internal framework types or adapting a JSON converter.

The public experience follows System.Text.Json (STJ) idioms: typed contracts, serializer contexts, options, resolvers, attributes, and composable generated definitions. The semantics are specific to form data, which consists of named string values and files rather than JSON tokens. A standalone generator supports explicit C# contexts; Razor owns Blazor form-model discovery across `.razor` and `.cs` inputs and supplies the same contracts without a competing discovery pipeline.

STJ supplies metadata/provider idioms, not feature parity. The feature covers existing form-mapping capabilities and the form-specific additions described here, without automatic naming transformations or unrelated STJ-style options.

## Goals

1. **Make complex form models usable with Native AOT and full trimming.** Supported Blazor and Minimal API forms must run with reflection-based form metadata discovery and runtime code generation disabled. The same submitted fields, files, contract, and read settings must produce equivalent values and mapping errors through generated and compatibility metadata.

2. **Make form contracts explicit and customizable.** Developers must be able to rename, exclude, require, construct, and convert supported model properties using form-owned attributes and metadata APIs. Form models must support ordinary objects, records, value types, supported collections and dictionaries, recursive models, and uploaded files without importing MVC's complete binder model or duplicating STJ's optional features.

3. **Make input interpretation deliberate.** Parsing uses invariant culture by default with a supported property-level current-culture opt-in, not a global setting. Missing input, empty input, repeated values, numeric collection indexing, and bracketed dictionary keys have documented semantics; custom converters handle alternative representations. In particular, a nullable custom value object must be able to interpret an empty field as null without a string-proxy property.

4. **Make failures actionable without discarding useful data.** Invalid contracts must identify the offending type/member before request handling when statically knowable. Invalid submitted data must expose structured field errors and retain successfully mapped data where construction is possible, enabling Blazor redisplay and explicit Minimal API error handling.

5. **Support framework and library composition without forcing migration.** Application and library definitions must compose through the same contracts. Existing applications retain a supported compatibility path; adopting the new API must not require changing HTTP form encodings, Blazor form routing, or the application's validation framework.

## Non-goals

1. **Writing objects into form fields or HTTP bodies.** This feature reads form data. It does not define serialization order, output omission, file upload production, or round-trip equivalence.

## Proposed solution

`Microsoft.AspNetCore.FormData` supplies public runtime contracts independent of the Components implementation namespace. Consumers can use it directly or through Blazor and Minimal API integration. The HTTP-facing input is an already-read `IFormCollection`, including its files; calling the serializer does not read or rewind a request body.

The public surface includes:

| Surface | Consumer responsibility and observable behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `FormDataSerializer` | Reads using a supplied typed contract, or options with a configured resolver. Provides a throwing convenience API and an error-collecting API. |
| `FormDataTypeInfo<T>` / `FormDataTypeInfo` | Describes the effective form shape and executable mapping capability for a type. Child types, members, constructor parameters, collection elements, and dictionary keys/values are represented without requiring consumers to obtain reflected members. |
| `FormDataPropertyInfo` / `FormDataParameterInfo` | Exposes effective field names, exclusion, presence requirements, conversion policy, and construction/assignment associations. Occurrence-level settings can differ for two properties of the same CLR type. |
| `FormDataSerializerContext` | Supplies generated definitions for explicitly declared roots and their required reachable types. |
| `IFormDataTypeInfoResolver` / `FormDataTypeInfoResolver` | Resolves type contracts and composes application, library, and optional reflection providers in a documented order. |
| `FormDataSerializerOptions` | Configures contract resolution and converters. A contract is associated with its options; mutable options are not shared across unrelated applications. It supplies no naming transformations or global value/culture policies. |
| `FormDataReadOptions` | Supplies root prefix, mapping limits, and diagnostic retention without changing cached contracts. Culture selection is not an operation setting. |
| `FormDataResult<T>` / `FormDataError` | Reports `Success`, `NoData`, or `InvalidData`, whether a value was produced, a possibly partial value, and structured field errors. |
| `FormDataConverter<T>` | Allows a custom scalar or structured form representation using public form-reader and error-reporting contracts. It is not a JSON converter or an MVC binder. |

Contract customization happens before use. Contracts and their associated serializer options become read-only when used or explicitly frozen. A resolver modifier can customize generated definitions as well as reflection-provided definitions; it cannot mutate an already-used contract.

The attributes describe the capabilities and precedence rules below.

| Annotation | Purpose and scope |
| --- | --- |
| `FormDataSerializable(typeof(T))` | Declares an explicit generated context root. |
| `FormDataSourceGenerationOptions` | Declares generation-time defaults and strict generated-only expectations for a context. It supplies no global culture choice and does not bake a request's current culture into generated metadata. |
| `FormDataPropertyName("field-name")` | Selects one literal form-name segment for a supported property or constructor parameter instead of its CLR name. |
| `FormDataIgnore` | Excludes a property from reading, like the existing legacy exclusion annotation. No conditional-ignore modes are introduced. |
| `FormDataRequired` | Requires submitted input for a member or constructor parameter. This is presence, not DataAnnotations validation. |
| `FormDataConstructor` | Selects one construction entry point when public constructor selection is ambiguous. |
| `FormDataUseCurrentCulture` | Opts a scalar property or that property's scalar collection elements into current-culture parsing. Unannotated properties remain invariant. The setting belongs to property metadata, including when the property is associated with a constructor parameter. |
| `FormDataEmptyStringHandling(...)` | Selects `Preserve`, `AsNull`, or `Reject` for a scalar member/parameter or that member's scalar collection elements. Whitespace-only text is not automatically empty. |
| `FormDataConverter(typeof(...))` | Selects a custom converter at type or member/parameter scope. |

Attributes describe the contract. Resolver APIs must allow equivalent customization for types an application cannot annotate. No attribute is required merely to preserve a public settable property's CLR name.

Examples below are independent consumer-code fragments, not one combined program. Contexts such as `BookingFormContext` and `OrderFormContext` follow the explicit root declaration shown in the first scenario; the referenced converter classes are application-supplied types.

### Read a simple form with a generated context

An application declares a model and an explicit context, then reads an already-parsed form using strongly typed metadata.

```csharp
public sealed class ContactInput
{
    public string? Name { get; set; }
    public int Age { get; set; }
}

[FormDataSerializable(typeof(ContactInput))]
internal partial class ContactFormContext : FormDataSerializerContext
{
}

ContactInput? contact = FormDataSerializer.Deserialize(
    form, ContactFormContext.Default.ContactInput);
```

`Name=Ana&Age=42` produces the corresponding values. Names match ordinally without case sensitivity by default. `Age=abc` causes `Deserialize` to throw a `FormDataException` containing mapping errors; it does not return a successfully populated object containing an unexplained default age.

The generated context covers supported types reachable from `ContactInput`. No runtime model discovery is needed to read the form.

### Adopt the contracts in Minimal APIs and Blazor

Applications can register shared form-data options and generated contexts while keeping their existing host entry points.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddFormData(options =>
    options.TypeInfoResolverChain.Add(ContactFormContext.Default));

app.MapPost("/contacts", ContactHandlers.Create);
```

`ContactHandlers.Create` has a `[FromForm] ContactInput` parameter. With the new integration enabled, both the runtime endpoint path and the Request Delegate Generator use the registered contract. Supported complex input no longer causes the generator to skip the endpoint because form mapping requires dynamic code.

```csharp
[GenerateFormDataMetadata]
public partial class ContactComponent : ComponentBase
{
    [SupplyParameterFromForm]
    private ContactInput Input { get; set; } = new();
}
```

Razor-owned Blazor generation discovers receiver types from component declarations and their base classes across Razor and C# inputs. The example uses a C# component declaration; equivalent Razor declarations receive the same form-contract support. Generated definitions are composed through the resolver chain; the developer does not maintain a second root list. Private nested models remain private when legally accessible from their generated context. Unsupported declarations and collisions produce compile-time diagnostics. Components that do not opt into the new path retain their existing behavior. Explicit library contexts can supply definitions for types they own; discovery does not silently replace such definitions.

Components use ordinary or enhanced named `EditForm` instances with the same supported form reading and mapping-error behavior. Explicit C# contexts and Blazor-discovered form roots target the same contracts.

Existing `[FromForm(Name = ...)]` field selectors, `[SupplyParameterFromForm(Name = ..., FormName = ...)]`, and form scopes retain their supported host roles. These selectors are not renamed to FormData attributes. In the current Minimal API complex-model path, FromForm.Name does not select a nested model prefix: complex properties are read from the empty model root. Preserve that behavior rather than introduce a new prefixed complex-binding feature. Direct core reads can select an explicit root prefix; host adaptation must not assume every host interprets its name selector as that prefix. The core reader does not route a form to a component.

Registration and activation must be explicit for existing applications. This proposal does not silently switch an existing application's mapper semantics merely because an updated framework contains the new assembly. Generated model availability and selection of the new runtime path are separate concerns.

### Rename, ignore, and require members

Today a shared-mapper model can use `DataMember` and `IgnoreDataMember`, but has no form-owned equivalents or public contract customization. The new annotations provide a form-specific vocabulary.

```csharp
public sealed class ContactInput
{
    [FormDataPropertyName("first_name")]
    [FormDataRequired]
    public string? FirstName { get; set; }

    [FormDataIgnore]
    public bool IsAdministrator { get; set; }

    public string? CampaignCode { get; set; }
}
```

`first_name=Ana&IsAdministrator=true&CampaignCode=autumn` sets `FirstName` and `CampaignCode`, but never assigns `IsAdministrator`. Missing `first_name` is a presence error; `first_name=` is present and must be considered separately by empty-value policy and validation. Public instance properties with public setters and constructor-associated properties retain the supported mapper model. Fields, non-public model accessors, static members, and indexers are not newly included.

Names are unchanged CLR names unless explicitly overridden by FormDataPropertyName or applicable DataMember.Name. There is no global naming policy, automatic casing transformation, or custom naming-policy hook. Two mapped properties whose effective names collide under the existing case-insensitive name matching make the contract invalid; the generator identifies both properties. Constructor/property associations use CLR identity, not renamed form-field text.

Names containing spaces, hyphens, underscores, and non-Latin characters are supported. In the dotted/bracketed grammar, `.`, `[` and `]` are structural characters and cannot be literal member-name segments; such an attribute is diagnosed rather than reinterpreted as a path. A custom converter is required for a different path grammar or a dictionary-key representation that includes those delimiters.

Renaming the read contract does not automatically rewrite existing rendered input names. The form must submit the effective name, for example `<input name="first_name">`. Changing Blazor's existing input-name generation is not silently included in this feature; metadata exposes effective names for hosts and components that deliberately integrate them.

### Preserve legacy annotations without interpreting JSON or MVC member annotations

Before adoption, an existing shared-mapper model can express these settings with legacy annotations:

```csharp
public sealed class LegacyInput
{
    [DataMember(Name = "first_name", IsRequired = true)]
    public string? FirstName { get; set; }

    [IgnoreDataMember]
    public string? ServerOnly { get; set; }
}
```

After adoption, that same model can retain those annotations or use the form-owned equivalents:

```csharp
public sealed class LegacyInput
{
    [FormDataPropertyName("first_name")]
    [FormDataRequired]
    public string? FirstName { get; set; }

    [FormDataIgnore]
    public string? ServerOnly { get; set; }
}
```

The new contract recognizes `DataMember.Name`, `DataMember.IsRequired`, and `IgnoreDataMember`. `DataMember.IsRequired` applies even when no name is supplied. C# required-member metadata also expresses an input-presence requirement unless the selected constructor is declared to satisfy required members. `DataContract` does not turn the model into a DataContract serializer, and `DataMember.Order` and `EmitDefaultValue` have no reading semantics.

Precedence is: explicit resolver customization, form-owned annotation for the same setting, applicable legacy annotation, convention. Exclusion is evaluated before resolving an excluded property's type. Either FormDataIgnore or IgnoreDataMember excludes the property; no inclusion or conditional-ignore annotation overrides it. Explicit metadata customization can describe the effective supported-property contract without annotations. Conflicting explicit form annotations that cannot be reconciled are contract errors.

`JsonPropertyName`, `JsonIgnore`, `JsonConstructor`, `JsonRequired`, `JsonConverter`, and MVC member-level `FromForm`, `BindNever`, and `BindRequired` do not customize the new contract. Generation reports a targeted warning when such a binding-looking annotation would otherwise be the only indication of the developer's intended form customization. It does not warn on unrelated validation/display attributes. Root-level host selectors remain supported as described above.

### Opt into current-culture parsing

Today the inspected shared complex-form paths pass invariant culture, and the conversion classes needed to change that are internal. The new API keeps invariant culture as the default and supports only one built-in alternative: current parsing culture, selected on an individual property. Serializer options, read options, and generation defaults do not select culture.

```csharp
public sealed class BookingInput
{
    [FormDataUseCurrentCulture]
    public decimal Amount { get; set; }

    public DateOnly TravelDate { get; set; }
}

BookingInput? booking = FormDataSerializer.Deserialize(
    form, BookingFormContext.Default.BookingInput);
```

When the application's current culture is fr-FR, `Amount=1,25&TravelDate=2026-12-31` produces `1.25m` and December 31, 2026. Without `FormDataUseCurrentCulture`, a property remains invariant. Equivalent property-metadata customization supports types an application cannot annotate. The property's policy also applies when its value supplies an associated constructor parameter; it is not an independent parameter-level culture setting. Property settings apply to that scalar conversion or its scalar collection elements, not indiscriminately to an entire nested object graph. Root scalar values remain invariant unless an explicit converter supplies different behavior.

Current culture is resolved for each read, not when a contract is generated or first cached. `CurrentUICulture` controls message localization, not the interpretation of numbers and dates. The form-data API does not expose a named-culture string or an arbitrary `CultureInfo` setting.

HTML date, time, and number controls can submit machine-formatted invariant values even when their visible UI is localized. Applications must be able to keep those members invariant while parsing localized free-text members in the same form. Explicit formats not expressible by culture alone use a custom converter. Collection indexes and default bracketed dictionary keys remain invariant; changing a value's culture never changes the structural grammar.

No automatic culture fallback is attempted after a parse fails. Posted hidden fields cannot change the invariant/current choice or override the contract; MVC's `__Invariant` convention is not implicitly adopted. Applications needing another culture or an exact format use an explicit converter rather than expanding this built-in attribute.

### Distinguish missing, empty, null, and invalid input

An optional domain value can choose null-on-empty explicitly.

```csharp
public sealed class BookingInput
{
    [FormDataEmptyStringHandling(FormDataEmptyStringHandling.AsNull)]
    public BookingCode? Code { get; set; }

    [FormDataEmptyStringHandling(FormDataEmptyStringHandling.Reject)]
    public string? Reference { get; set; }
}
```

`BookingCode` denotes a custom struct with a supported parser or registered converter. `Code=` produces null without invoking a parser that can only return a non-nullable `BookingCode`. `Reference=` is an empty-input error. `Code=bad` is a conversion error, not null-on-failure.

| Input state | Required behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Member absent | Do not assign a settable property; preserve its initializer. Report a presence error if required. Constructor defaults follow the construction rules below. |
| Present empty string | Apply the member's empty-string policy before scalar conversion. An explicit `AsNull` is invalid for a non-nullable value target. |
| Present whitespace | Pass through unchanged unless a converter explicitly trims it. Do not equate whitespace with absence. |
| Explicit null | Ordinary form fields have no null token. The string `"null"` is text, not null. A converter can define another representation explicitly. |
| Invalid nonempty value | Record a field conversion error. Do not claim successful conversion to `default(T)`. |

Defaults preserve strings, use null-on-empty for the built-in nullable scalar types supported by the legacy mapper, and delegate other scalar conversion to its parser. Custom nullable structs retain that default delegation for compatibility but can opt into `AsNull`, resolving the gap identified in #69901. Required-input presence does not add nullable-reference-annotation enforcement; DataAnnotations validation remains a later stage. Empty-value overrides belong to property/parameter metadata rather than a global serializer default.

Built-in scalar coverage includes strings, characters, Boolean values, signed/unsigned integer types including 128-bit types, floating-point types including `Half`, `decimal`, `Guid`, `DateOnly`, `TimeOnly`, `DateTime`, `DateTimeOffset`, `TimeSpan`, `Uri`, enums, and nullable forms of supported value types. Other `IParsable<T>` implementations are supported. Enum reading follows the current case-insensitive name/numeric parsing convention, including comma-separated flag names and representable numeric values; rejection of unnamed numeric values or custom enum spellings requires an explicit converter. Multidimensional arrays, open generic types, and unconfigured abstract/interface object models are not implicitly supported.

For a root with no matching submitted fields or files, the collecting API returns `NoData`, `HasValue = false`, and no mapping errors. The convenience API returns its default value for that absence. A host requiring a model must handle `NoData` explicitly; unrelated antiforgery and handler fields do not manufacture a model. An unchecked checkbox that produces no field is absence, not an instruction to assign false. Hosts and form controls retain responsibility for any hidden false-value convention.

For the new host integration, a required Minimal API form parameter with `NoData` is a bad request and the normal handler is not invoked; an optional parameter receives its declared default or null. A Blazor form receiver with `NoData` keeps an already initialized value rather than having it overwritten by a fabricated mapped default. If that receiver explicitly requires submitted input, absence is surfaced as a mapping requirement error. These host outcomes do not turn an omitted checkbox into an explicit false value.

### Construct immutable models and resolve constructor ambiguity

Without explicit selection, the legacy single-public-constructor convention remains available. A model with multiple public constructors can opt into a selected construction entry point instead of silently binding null.

```csharp
public sealed record ReservationInput(
    [property: FormDataPropertyName("guest_name")] string GuestName,
    int Seats = 1);
```

`guest_name=Ana` produces a reservation for one seat. The effective form name is shared by the constructor parameter and its associated property; the member is not mapped twice. Parameter-to-property matching uses CLR name and type, with case-insensitive name matching. An explicit parameter annotation overrides the associated property's setting; otherwise applicable property settings flow to the parameter.

`[FormDataConstructor]` on one supported constructor selects it when multiple constructors exist. No selected constructor and multiple public constructors is an actionable contract error. Required constructor parameters must be present; parameters with explicit defaults use those defaults when absent unless explicitly marked required. A missing required argument prevents invocation, yields `InvalidData`, and produces no instance of that containing object.

Constructor exceptions become mapping errors associated with the object's path, with safe client-facing text and the underlying exception available to application diagnostics. They are not mistaken for missing metadata. Construction follows the supported public-constructor model. No new private-constructor, field, or non-public model-accessor inclusion capability is introduced; explicit custom converters can implement application-specific construction.

Required C# construction assignments follow the same rule as required constructor arguments: when such a slot has no successfully mapped value, neither generated nor reflection execution constructs that containing instance. The result remains invalid with the corresponding presence/conversion error rather than inventing a default required assignment to make generated source compile. Successfully mapped nullable values still count as values. This does not turn optional properties into required slots or permit overwriting absent optional initializers.

Read-only computed properties are excluded unless associated with construction. `init` members are supported when the generated or explicitly supplied contract can initialize them; unsupported construction/access combinations identify the member. This feature constructs new models rather than updating an existing object graph.

### Bind collections with predictable numeric indexes

Collections accept repeated scalar values (`Tags=one&Tags=two`) or consecutive numeric paths (`Lines[0].Quantity=2&Lines[1].Quantity=3`) without a collection-specific annotation.

```csharp
public sealed class OrderInput
{
    public List<OrderLineInput>? Lines { get; set; }
}
```

`Lines[0].Quantity=2&Lines[1].Quantity=3` produces two items in numeric-index order. Mixed repeated/indexed representations and invalid numeric indexes produce field errors. A gap followed by more submitted items is an error rather than silent truncation. These grammar rules apply to the new contract; legacy host behavior is not silently rewritten. Named `.index` protocols are not a built-in feature in this release; an application can implement one with a custom converter.

Scalar conversion failure in one element does not prevent diagnostics for later submitted elements. Mutable sequences, arrays, sets, queues, stacks, and immutable/read-only collection targets supported by the current mapper remain representable; sequence targets preserve logical element order, while sets and unordered collections retain their own semantics. Custom collection construction can be supplied through public contracts or converters. Recursive item types terminate based on actual input presence, not the mere availability of a child contract.

Required targets are one-dimensional arrays; concrete `ICollection<T>` types with public parameterless constructors; `Queue<T>`, `Stack<T>`, `ReadOnlyCollection<T>`; concurrent bag/queue/stack; immutable array/list/hash-set/sorted-set/queue/stack; and the standard generic enumerable, collection, list, set, read-only collection/list/set, and immutable list/set/queue/stack interfaces. Interface targets select the corresponding standard list, set, or immutable representation; they do not activate an arbitrary application implementation. A custom type outside this list needs an explicitly supplied contract or converter.

### Bind dictionaries without truncating keys

The built-in dictionary format is `Values[key]=value`, with invariant key conversion and ordinal case-sensitive string-key identity. Form path matching is still case-insensitive; distinct entries that become ambiguous under that matching are rejected rather than arbitrarily combined.

This guarantee applies to identities still distinguishable in the supplied IFormCollection. An HTTP parser may already have combined case-equivalent field names into one StringValues entry; the mapper cannot recover original spelling or occurrences from that normalized input. Preserve that parser boundary and existing first-scalar-value behavior rather than introduce raw body parsing to infer lost key identities.

```csharp
public sealed class LabelsInput
{
    public Dictionary<string, int>? Values { get; set; }
}
```

`Values[category]=2` produces the string key `category` with value two. No dictionary-specific annotation is required.

Unmatched or ambiguous delimiters such as `Values[x]y]=2` are a malformed-path error; the reader never substitutes key `x` and default value zero. Duplicate converted keys and invalid key conversion are errors. A custom key converter can extend scalar key conversion, but cannot change the built-in path grammar. Keys containing structural delimiters or a key/value-entry protocol require an explicit structured converter; no built-in dictionary-format selector is proposed.

Required dictionary targets are `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`, sorted dictionary/list, concurrent dictionary, read-only dictionary, immutable dictionary/sorted dictionary, the standard dictionary/read-only dictionary/immutable dictionary interfaces, and concrete `IDictionary<TKey, TValue>` types with public parameterless constructors. Bracketed keys use `ISpanParsable<TKey>` by default; an explicit form key converter can extend that set. Key conversion remains invariant unless an explicit key converter supplies another interpretation.

### Bind files consistently at roots and nested paths

The form-data contract distinguishes uploaded files from text values. Core support includes `IFormFile`, named `IFormFile[]`, `List<IFormFile>` and `IReadOnlyList<IFormFile>`, and `IFormFileCollection`. Named sequences read multiple files submitted under the same field name; a custom converter can implement indexed file paths rather than a built-in collection-format selector.

```csharp
public sealed class OrderLineInput
{
    public int Quantity { get; set; }
    public IReadOnlyList<IFormFile>? Attachments { get; set; }
}
```

Files posted as `Lines[0].Attachments` attach only to that member. No matching files do not manufacture another collection item or keep an indexed collection alive indefinitely. A root named file sequence respects the host-selected parameter name or explicit root name; an all-files target is not silently treated as a named sequence, or vice versa.

At a root, `IFormFileCollection` means all files supplied by the caller, independent of the model-name prefix. At a nested member it means files matching that member's full field name, with absence when none match. This explicit nested scoping differs from the current converter's unconditional all-files return and must be documented as an adoption change. A caller that needs an all-request file collection inside each child object supplies an explicit converter; that converter's availability does not establish that a child item exists.

File-only input counts as model data. Text and files in different nested members can be mapped together. A text field and a file with the same path are distinct input channels interpreted by the target contract. Blazor can supply its `IBrowserFile` integration without making the core assembly depend on Components. Reading a file reference does not copy, persist, or validate file contents.

### Supply a custom converter without changing the model to strings

Applications can register a converter for a type or one occurrence.

```csharp
var options = new FormDataSerializerOptions
{
    TypeInfoResolver = BookingFormContext.Default
};
options.Converters.Add(new BookingCodeFormConverter());

BookingInput? booking =
    FormDataSerializer.Deserialize<BookingInput>(form, options);
```

```csharp
public sealed class BookingInput
{
    [FormDataConverter(typeof(IsoWeekDateFormConverter))]
    public DateOnly WeekDate { get; set; }
}
```

The referenced classes are application implementations of the proposed `FormDataConverter<T>` contract; converter implementations are intentionally not specified here. A converter can read a scalar's submitted values or a structured subtree, distinguish absent input from invalid input, use the effective culture, delegate a child to another resolved contract, and report errors at a child path. It must not bypass operation limits or access another root's scope. A custom scalar converter remains usable for repeated collection values and dictionary values.

Precedence is member/parameter converter, type annotation converter, ordered options converters, then built-in conversion. `IParsable<T>` is supported without an explicit converter. Arbitrary MVC `TypeConverter` discovery, `BindAsync`, MVC binders, and existing JSON converters are not automatically invoked; applications provide a form adapter explicitly where needed.

A converter for a base class can implement an application's allowlisted discriminator protocol. This does not imply built-in `JsonDerivedType` support. User code bugs and invalid converter contracts remain developer-visible exceptions; the reader does not convert arbitrary programming failures into successful default values.

### Compose application and library definitions

A library can expose a generated context, and an application can combine it with its own.

```csharp
var options = new FormDataSerializerOptions
{
    TypeInfoResolver = FormDataTypeInfoResolver.Combine(
        ApplicationFormContext.Default,
        LibraryFormContext.Default)
};
```

Resolvers are queried in order and the first non-null type definition wins. Contracts for the same CLR type are not merged. The options-based overload resolves child contracts through the effective composed options so nested customizations remain consistent. Direct typed-contract overloads use that contract's associated options and reject incompatible use instead of silently applying unrelated options.

Library definitions describe the types they own; composition does not require runtime assembly scanning. For a known form root, all required reachable type definitions and converters must be available. Recursive references do not require infinitely many generated definitions. An explicitly ignored unsupported member does not make its containing type unsupported.

Strict execution includes only generated or explicitly supplied definitions. Reflection compatibility is an explicitly selectable provider for applications that permit it, not an implicit fallback when a generated contract is missing. Build-time completeness checks apply to statically known roots; runtime-supplied resolver/converter configurations are checked when the contract is first resolved or registered, before a request handler receives its value.

For an application that intentionally permits reflection, `new DefaultFormDataTypeInfoResolver()` is the proposed explicit compatibility provider and can be added last in the resolver chain. Strict mode rejects registration of that provider. A generated-context-only chain is usable directly without registering a reflection provider or maintaining a second serialization model.

### Collect errors and retain partial values

An application can read without throwing for expected input failures.

```csharp
FormDataResult<OrderInput> result =
    FormDataSerializer.DeserializeWithErrors(
        form, OrderFormContext.Default.OrderInput);
```

For an `OrderInput` using default numeric indexes, `Lines[0].Quantity=abc&Lines[1].Quantity=3` produces `InvalidData`; it includes a conversion error for the first quantity and retains the successfully read second quantity where the declared construction permits a partial model. Default values in failed slots are never evidence of success: `Status` and `Errors` must be checked. `HasValue` distinguishes a produced value, including a successful null, from no produced instance.

Each error supplies a stable category, submitted field path, target member identity where applicable, a safe message, and the attempted text value when the application requests its retention. Categories include missing required input, invalid value, disallowed empty/null, duplicate value/key, malformed path, and exceeded limit. File contents are never retained in an error. Attempted values are not automatically written to logs or responses.

Blazor associates errors with the correct nested instance and form field for redisplay. Minimal API automatic parameter binding retains its bad-request behavior for invalid submitted input and does not invoke a normal handler with a success-shaped default; applications wanting partial results use the collecting API explicitly inside their handler. The core result is not MVC `ModelState` and does not claim that validation has run. Validation can subsequently append errors through host integration without erasing mapping errors.

`NoData` is not a conversion error. Conversely, an unresolved type, invalid constructor contract, invalid options, or missing strict-mode definition is a configuration failure, not `NoData` or an empty successful result. Contract failures identify the root and failing member/type and recommend supplying a definition, converter, valid construction choice, or exclusion.

### Bound resource use and reject ambiguous input

Applications can bound mapping independently of HTTP request-body parsing.

```csharp
var readOptions = new FormDataReadOptions
{
    MaxCollectionSize = 1024,
    MaxRecursionDepth = 64,
    MaxErrorCount = 200,
    MaxKeySize = 2048
};
```

These are the library default limits shown explicitly. `MaxCollectionSize` applies to every collection and dictionary representation, including repeated scalar values and files; `MaxRecursionDepth` bounds nested traversal; `MaxKeySize` bounds a decoded submitted path. `MaxErrorCount` bounds retained diagnostics, including one terminal truncation diagnostic. Limits must be positive, and a depth limit must permit at least the root and one child. Exceeding a limit makes the operation invalid; it never becomes a silently successful truncated model.

Retain existing behavior: scalar targets use the first submitted value and unknown members are ignored. No duplicate-scalar or unknown-member policy selector is introduced. Collection repetition is not a duplicate scalar error; duplicate converted dictionary keys remain errors. Explicitly ignored properties are never assigned. Hosts keep antiforgery/routing metadata outside selected model data.

Path-prefix checks are segment-aware: selecting `Order` does not select `OrderOther`. Exceeding limits in custom converters is subject to the same result and reporting rules. Invalid option values fail before reading input. HTTP field-count, multipart/body-size, and file-size limits remain separate host protections and are not disabled by these options.

### Preserve existing applications and expose intentional behavior changes

Before adoption, existing applications keep their supported form-mapping path and documented host defaults. After explicit adoption, the new API's generated and compatibility providers follow one contract semantics; reflection does not mean "use different binding rules."

Intentional new-contract requirements include honoring optional constructor defaults, preserving absent settable-member initializers, reporting constructor ambiguity, applying `DataMember.IsRequired` without requiring a rename, rejecting sparse numeric input instead of losing later items, scoping nested file collections, and diagnosing malformed dictionary paths. These are not described as byte-for-byte compatibility with the current mapper. Migration documentation must show how to retain old application behavior where it was intentional, or identify a behavior change that requires application action.

Form-owned annotations take effect only on the new contract path. Existing annotation-only models remain usable through the supported legacy path while adopting the new assembly is evaluated. Nothing in this proposal removes a reflection path required by existing applications.

# Fix contrast of Identity instructional text

Use inherited body color for Identity instructional text.

## Description

Bootstrap's `text-info` gives normal-sized Identity instructions insufficient contrast on white: approximately 1.96:1 in Bootstrap 5 and 3.05:1 in Bootstrap 4, below the required 4.5:1. Remove the class so these paragraphs inherit the readable surrounding text color, without changing the global Bootstrap palette or relying on a Bootstrap 5-only utility.

The fix covers Blazor Set Password instructions, the shared reauthentication prompt used by Set Password and Passkeys, and Bootstrap 4/5 Identity UI Set Password and external-login registration instructions. Wording, forms, IDs, and authentication behavior are unchanged.

Extend the existing Identity functional page checks to reject the failing class, and the existing Blazor credential-reauthentication browser test to check that all three affected paragraphs inherit the body color.

### Accessibility criterion and visual comparison

[WCAG 2.2 Contrast (Minimum), SC 1.4.3 (Level AA)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) requires:

> The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.

These instructional paragraphs are normal-sized text, so the large-text exception does not apply. `text-info` only applies a visual color; it does not provide accessibility semantics. The instructions retain their informational meaning without cyan.

| Light-mode text on white | Before | After | Required |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Blazor and Bootstrap 5 Identity UI | 1.96:1 | 15.43:1 | 4.5:1 |
| Bootstrap 4 Identity UI | 3.05:1 | 15.43:1 | 4.5:1 |

These are direct screenshots of `/Account/Manage/SetPassword` in a generated Blazor Web App (`--auth Individual --interactivity Server`), using the locally built templates and runtime. Both versions use Chromium at 1280 x 960, the same account state, and the normal template layout. The before copy retains the original `text-info` attributes; the after copy uses this fix. No diagnostic panels, overlays, or injected color changes are used.

**Set Password page after confirming identity**

Issues.Title: Support Native AOT and full trimming in Blazor
Issues.Body:
# Summary

This feature enables Blazor applications to publish and run with Native AOT and full trimming across the supported application model, without relying on reflection-based discovery or runtime code generation. It makes native deployment practical and creates opportunities to reduce startup, application size, memory use, and repeated runtime work.

The work introduces composable application and library metadata, build-time generation through Razor, and trim-safe contracts for serialization and form mapping. Component execution, routing, JavaScript interop, persistence, binding, and forms consume the resulting capabilities. Existing applications retain a supported compatibility path, while strict applications get explicit diagnostics rather than silent reflection fallbacks.

## Goals

1. **Make Native AOT and full trimming usable without removing supported functionality.** Representative applications must publish with zero trimming and ILC warnings and exercise their claimed scenarios without framework reflection fallbacks, runtime code generation, broad warning suppressions, or substitutions that remove those scenarios.

2. **Make application and library contributions composable.** Applications, framework assemblies, and component libraries must supply the definitions their features need. Hosts and consumers must use the appropriate selected application without requiring HTTP endpoint mapping, repeated assembly scanning, or application-side reconstruction of library internals.

3. **Make framework serialization and form mapping trim-safe.** Generated contracts must support form-data reading, .NET-to-.NET state serialization, and .NET-to-JavaScript interop with the distinct behavior each boundary requires. Supported customization must work without reflection-based contract discovery or runtime code generation.

4. **Preserve an undegraded upgrade experience.** Existing applications and libraries must continue to work without additional warnings or required AOT-related changes when upgrading without enabling additional AOT features or checks. Applications choosing strict execution must receive actionable errors for missing definitions and unsupported shapes instead of discovering incomplete support after deployment.

## Non-goals

1. **Require every existing application to adopt Native AOT.** Applications that do not enable additional AOT features or checks retain their existing supported experience without degradation. Upgrading alone must not introduce additional warnings or require AOT-related application changes.

2. **Support unrestricted runtime discovery in strict execution.** Types and behavior required at runtime must have AOT-compatible definitions. Missing definitions produce actionable diagnostics rather than reflection fallbacks.

## Proposed solution

Provide generated definitions for Blazor features that currently depend on runtime discovery or dynamically constructed accessors. Framework consumers use those definitions to support Native AOT and full trimming while preserving supported application behavior.

Razor owns Blazor generation across `.razor` and `.cs` inputs. Libraries contribute their own definitions, which compose with application definitions into a host-neutral application model. Consumers retrieve the features they need without scanning assemblies or reconstructing library internals. Generic metadata templates allow consumers to obtain definitions for statically known constructed types.

The work covers four areas:

1. **Serialization.** Provide trim-safe contracts for form-data reading, component descriptors, persisted values, and JavaScript interop. Preserve the distinct conversion, customization, and error behavior of each boundary.

2. **Discovery.** Supply definitions for components, routes, root-component mappings, component-associated metadata, JS-invokable methods, and persistent-service members. Root-component descriptors resolve through known mappings; JS-invokable methods use generated invocation support, including asynchronous completion.

3. **Component runtime.** Provide generated support for component construction, injection, and ordinary and cascading parameter assignment. Integrate the query-string, form, persistent-state, session, and TempData suppliers while preserving their individual delivery and lifecycle semantics.

4. **Forms and binding.** Provide attribute-value conversion and binding-target metadata without runtime converter discovery or expression inspection. Preserve value delivery and callbacks, field identity, submitted field paths, display names, and integration with existing validation.

Runtime decisions remain supported when they select definitions available ahead of time. A root parameter declared as `Person`, for example, may carry an `Employee`. Applications must be able to declare additional concrete root-parameter types that generation cannot otherwise establish, so their serialization definitions and descriptor mappings are available. The declaration's final API remains to be designed.

Component types must be public for the strict generated experience. Supported internal-member access includes injection and cascading-parameter delivery. Missing definitions and unsupported shapes produce actionable diagnostics rather than silent reflection fallbacks.

Applications upgrading without enabling additional AOT features or checks retain their supported experience without additional warnings or required AOT-related changes. Generation and strict execution are introduced without degrading that compatibility path.

The following scenarios define the intended experience. Existing entry points are illustrative; unapproved new API signatures are deliberately not invented.

### Publish an ordinary Blazor application with Native AOT

The application uses its normal component and host setup, then publishes for a supported native target:

```shell
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true
```

Its supported component, routing, interop, binding, persistence, and form scenarios execute correctly with the necessary generated definitions. Native publication produces no trimming or ILC warnings; removing functionality to satisfy that condition does not meet the requirement.

### Compose a component library without reproducing its internals

An application references a Razor class library and uses its components through the normal Razor experience. Component types must be public for the strict generated experience; internal members remain supported for injection and cascading-value/parameter delivery. The library supplies its own definitions, and the application does not maintain a second description of those members or scan the library at runtime in strict execution.

Repeated references to the same contributing library do not duplicate it. Different contributions that conflict are handled by a documented, deterministic policy rather than accidental registration order.

### Configure features and consume the same application in different hosts

An application continues to use host configuration such as:

```csharp
app.MapRazorComponents<App>()
    .AddInteractiveServerRenderMode();
```

The host extension can contribute or modify the relevant library features before finalization. Endpoint consumers, interactive routing, and non-HTTP rendering retrieve the features they need without introducing HTTP dependencies into Components core.

Separate mapped applications retain separate definitions. The selected application remains correct when work enters an Interactive Server circuit or a WebView page scope; an unrelated mapping or service provider must not replace it.

### Persist and restore application values

An application persists component or service state using supported framework APIs. Generated definitions cover the application values, and the framework can serialize and restore them without runtime type discovery.

Using generated serialization preserves the supported persistence and restoration behavior, including compatibility requirements for data that outlives a deployment.

### Use JavaScript interop with framework-owned values

Existing supported interop operations, including JavaScript-invokable methods and asynchronous results, execute without reflection-based method discovery or runtime generic construction. Element references, object references, streams, byte arrays, custom event values, and dynamic component parameters retain their supported behavior.

Generated contracts for an application object containing an ElementReference or JS object reference use the framework's handling of those values. Supported custom serialization must have an explicit AOT-compatible integration rather than depend on runtime member discovery.

### Read a complex submitted form

An existing Minimal API retains its form-bound handler shape, and a static SSR component retains its named form and SupplyParameterFromForm receiver. After adoption of the new contracts, generated form reading supports the required object construction, nested values, collections, files, conversion, limits, and mapping errors without runtime code generation.

Generated form-data contracts preserve the supported customization, conversion, culture, file, and error behavior of the adopted form-data API.

Explicit C# form contexts and Razor-discovered form roots produce the same supported contracts. The existing C#-only prototype increment does not, by itself, complete actual Razor integration or whole-Blazor Native AOT support.

### Diagnose an incomplete strict application

A required component definition, closed generic usage, interop method, or serialization/form contract is missing or unsupported. Statically knowable failures identify the affected type/member and corrective action during the build; unresolved runtime cases fail explicitly before an invalid operation can appear successful.

Strict execution never silently switches to reflection. Custom extensions are responsible for their own AOT compatibility; the framework does not promise to prove arbitrary developer code reflection-free.

### Adopt the changes without breaking an existing application

An application that upgrades without enabling additional AOT features or checks retains its supported reflection-compatible experience without degradation, additional warnings, or required AOT-related code or configuration changes. Validation compares its build and publish diagnostics before and after the upgrade; warnings must not be added merely because the new framework contains AOT support.

Applications opting into additional AOT features or checks receive the corresponding diagnostics. Adoption documentation explains generated-contract requirements, supported customization, library compatibility, and any intentional behavior changes on that opt-in path.

Generated and compatibility execution preserve the supported semantics for the same adopted contracts. Shared behavior remains correct across applicable Server, WebAssembly, WebView, static SSR, and non-HTTP scenarios; the native deployment acceptance suite uses supported native hosts.

Issues.Body:
<!-- flakiness-migration:mmitche/AspNetCore/1 -->

Copied from [mmitche/AspNetCore#1](https://github.com/mmitche/AspNetCore/issues/1) at the author's request because GitHub rejected a cross-owner issue transfer. The original report and discussion remain available there. This is a duplicate tracking report for [dotnet/aspnetcore#69494](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/69494), not a newly collected set of failures.

### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

The canonical issue is [dotnet/aspnetcore#69494](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/69494).

### Describe the bug

**Failure**

The `BlazorWebTemplate_ConditionalPasskeyRegistration` template test failed on three unrelated pull requests, interrupting their final CI iteration. The established failure in the canonical issue happens when the test reads an earlier response body after automatic navigation has made it unavailable.

**Possible cause**

The test captures the response, waits for later navigation and other checks, and only then reads its body; Chromium can discard that body during the interval. This mechanism is reproduced locally and documented in the canonical issue, but its association with the three CI occurrences below remains an inference because their retained test-result records lack the exact exception text.

**Affected builds and PRs**

| PR | PR target branch | Build(s) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| [dotnet/aspnetcore#70119](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70119) | `main` | [Failed build 1656560](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1656560); [same-iteration recovery build 1656681](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1656681) | Windows Release x64; `Templates.Blazor.Tests_net12.0_x64.html`; failed test result 46113304/100043 had no retained error text. |
| [dotnet/aspnetcore#70263](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70263) | `main` | [Failed attempt 1 and recovery attempt in build 1662505](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1662505) | Platform tests; Windows Release x64; failed test result 46293580/100051 had no retained error text. |
| [dotnet/aspnetcore#70108](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70108) | `main` | [Failed attempt 1 and recovery attempt in build 1657221](https://dev.azure.com/dnceng-public/public/_build/results?buildId=1657221) | Platform tests; Windows Release x64; failed test result 46131412/100043 had no retained error text. |

<!-- flakiness-occurrence:azuredevops/dnceng-public/public/83/build/1656681 -->
<!-- flakiness-occurrence:azuredevops/dnceng-public/public/83/build/1662505 -->
<!-- flakiness-occurrence:azuredevops/dnceng-public/public/83/build/1657221 -->

**Evidence**

The failed tasks reported `XUnit: Tests failed: ... Templates.Blazor.Tests_net12.0_x64.html`, and the only retained failed result in each occurrence was `BlazorWebTemplate_ConditionalPasskeyRegistration`. The exact exception text was unavailable in those three records. The PR target branches were verified from GitHub's PR base-branch metadata when copying this report.

### Expected Behavior

The test should retain the response text before automatic navigation makes the body unavailable, without changing the application's behavior or weakening its assertions.

### Steps To Reproduce

Run `BlazorWebTemplate_ConditionalPasskeyRegistration` with the passkey-upgrade flow. The known failure occurs when the first upgrade POST's response body is read after the page automatically submits its continuation and navigates. See the [canonical issue](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/69494) and [draft correction](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70362) for the mechanism and validation boundaries.

### Exceptions (if any)

The established issue and local browser reproduction exhibit:

```text
Microsoft.Playwright.PlaywrightException:
Protocol error (Network.getResponseBody): No resource with given identifier found
Response body is not available for a response that was navigated away from.
```

This is not a recovered excerpt from the three CI test-result records, whose exception text is missing.

### .NET Version

The recorded CI results target `net12.0`. The complete generated-application theory was not run locally because the repository's pinned .NET 12 SDK and matching product/template artifacts are absent.

### Anything else?

**Decision update**

The obsolete fork-base blocker in the original report has been removed. [Draft dotnet/aspnetcore#70362](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70362) saves the first upgrade POST's HTML before delivering it to the browser. Initial GETs and the continuation POST remain on the normal path, and the existing assertions are preserved; no production code, retry, delay, or timeout changes are proposed.

A bounded local Chromium experiment using the actual template continuation script reproduced the body-read error in 12/12 baseline runs and passed 12/12 with response capture. The exact added C# capture block also compiled against cached Playwright APIs. These checks support the proposed mechanism, not a claim that the full generated-application theory or CI remediation is verified.

The narrow test-only correction is worth review, but the complete theory still needs validation. This report is being consolidated as a duplicate, not closed as fixed. The [original follow-up discussion](https://github.com/mmitche/AspNetCore/issues/1#issuecomment-6689613075) retains the detailed review rationale and limitations.

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.

`.github/agents/review-candidate-verifier.agent.md:71-80` and `.github/skills/review-pull-request/SKILL.md:286-291, 333-336` specify 11 required output fields for `review-candidate-verifier` (`candidateId`, `decision`, `downgradeKind`, `dropBasis`, `contradictedLink`, `links`, `missingEvidence`, `correctedChangedLine`, `correctedRepro`, `validationEvidence`, `reason`, with 7 subfields under `links`), and `SKILL.md:334` instructs the orchestrator to treat any *"extra, duplicate, or schema-invalid verifier result"* as `INCOMPLETE`.

Because `review-candidate-verifier.agent.md:71-80` describes the 11 output fields in prose rather than providing an explicit strict JSON template that forbids extra keys or prose wrappers, two formatting failures occurred during live PR reviews:

1. **Cosmetic extra synonym key (`#70299` Round 2, `gpt-5.6-sol` verifier `263bcb8e`):**
   - When evaluating candidate `C1` (`NavigationEnhancement.ts:131`, `DROP / unestablished`) at commit `0317f5f729136a3a4f7320ab8bff3aa7d66fe5d6`, the verifier returned a valid JSON object containing all 11 required top-level keys and all 7 `links` boolean subfields, plus a 12th top-level key `"rationale"` duplicating `"reason"`. Under strict 11-key validation (`SKILL.md:334`), that extra key forced the arm to self-mark `INCOMPLETE` (`schema_invalid_verifier_output`) even though the substantive verification was complete and unambiguous.
2. **Markdown prose response instead of schema-complete JSON (`#70340` Round 1, `claude-opus-5.5` verifier `2b0c04c8`):**
   - When evaluating 2 candidates at commit `621bf279c3d882d691310044ca814aa4f924c2d5`, the verifier returned markdown prose `KEEP` sections with bulleted link descriptions instead of a JSON array/object containing `candidateId` and the 11 required keys.

### Describe the solution you'd like

1. **Add an explicit JSON schema / template in `.github/agents/review-candidate-verifier.agent.md`:**
   - Replace the prose-only field list at lines 71–80 with an explicit JSON structure showing the exact 11 top-level keys and 7 `links` boolean subfields, and explicitly forbid markdown prose wrappers or extra top-level keys (such as `"rationale"`, `"summary"`, or `"notes"`).
2. **Define bounded normalization and retry rules in `.github/skills/review-pull-request/SKILL.md`:**
   - Allow the orchestrator to ignore/strip benign extra top-level keys (such as `"rationale"` when `"reason"` and all 11 required keys + 7 `links` booleans are present and valid) without invalidating the review pass.
   - When a verifier response is missing required keys or returned as prose instead of JSON, allow one bounded format-only retry before failing closed as `INCOMPLETE`.
